name: incognito-window-has-no-spaces
description: Incognito is a profile property, not a window type, so an incognito window used to get the same sidebar as any other: the space rail, the dots, the active space's name, and its tabs written into that space. It must get none of them. Cmd+Shift+N opens the window, and the second sidebar document is read directly - both carry the same chrome://atrium/sidebar URL, so the incognito one names itself with a #incognito fragment or no probe could tell the two apart. Both targets are written as an exact path+fragment, which cdp-eval matches before it falls back to a substring - a bare '/sidebar' would otherwise match either document. The regular window is read first, while it is still the only sidebar, and its rail/dots/name are the control: without it 'no rail' passes on a sidebar that never drew. The fixture's two rows are named in the leak check, because 'the window shows some rows' does not say they are its own.

actions.expression: (() => { const has = (s) => document.querySelector(s) ? 'yes' : 'no'; return 'rail=' + has('.rail') + ' dots=' + has('.spacedots') + ' name=' + has('.wsname'); })()
actions.note: The control, read while this is still the only sidebar document. An incognito window drawing none of these means nothing unless an ordinary one draws all three.
The class apply() sets after a push, so this waits for a rendered sidebar rather than a loaded document.

actions.expression: (() => { const b = document.querySelector('.newtab'); if (!b) { return 'no button'; } b.click(); return 'clicked'; })()
actions.note: An incognito window opens with no tabs, so it needs one of its own before 'only its own tabs' can be read at all.

actions.expression: (() => { const has = (s) => document.querySelector(s) ? 'yes' : 'no'; const titles = [...document.querySelectorAll('.tabrow .tl')].map((n) => n.textContent); const leaked = titles.some((t) => t === 'Crimson Left' || t === 'Blue Left'); const zone = document.querySelector('.rows'); const drag = zone && (zone.dataset.dropzone || [...document.querySelectorAll('.tabrow')].some((r) => r.draggable)); return 'rail=' + has('.rail') + ' dots=' + has('.spacedots') + ' name=' + has('.wsname') + ' rows=' + (titles.length ? 'some' : 'none') + ' leaked=' + (leaked ? 'yes' : 'no') + ' drag=' + (drag ? 'yes' : 'no'); })()

actions.note: The page-side guards only decide what is DRAWN. A renderer sends any name it likes, so the refusal has to be measured on the browser side - this fires the message the hidden drag would have sent.

assertions.desc: the control: an ordinary window still draws its rail, its dots and its space name
the second window really built and rendered a sidebar of its own
the incognito sidebar is live, so the row count below is a real reading
THE MEASUREMENT: no rail, no dots, no space name, its own tab drawn, neither of the fixture space's rows in sight, and no row a drag could file into a space
the write message really left the renderer, so the drop below is the browser refusing it rather than nothing having happened

assertions.label: route-gate-fired
assertions.pattern: Atrium: surface message dropped, window is off the record: [s]idebarTabReordered
assertions.desc: THE OTHER HALF: a hand-sent write message reached the dispatcher and was refused there, which is the only guard a renderer cannot walk past. The [s] is a one-character class, not a typo - the message name is interpolated into that log line, so the pre-run source check needs a wildcard to stop the literal at.

assertions.label: write-guard-fired
assertions.pattern: Atrium: tab [0-9]+ not persisted, window is off the record
assertions.desc: the tab reached the write path and was refused there, rather than never being opened

assertions.label: flat-model-served
assertions.pattern: Atrium: sidebar model is the FLAT TAB LIST - off the record
assertions.desc: the core never answered for this window, so no space's rows were ever built for it
Cmd+Q still quits cleanly with the incognito window open
